chunks: "A SAR ADC does a binary search. It has a sample-and-hold that freezes the input, a comparator, a small internal DAC, and a register that holds the code under test.
It starts with the MSB. The register is set to 1000.. which makes the DAC output half of the reference. The comparator asks, 'Is my input above this?'
If yes, the 1 stays; if no, it's cleared to 0. Then it tries the next bit by setting it to 1, the DAC output moves by a quarter of the reference, and the comparator decides again.
After N comparisons, one per bit, the register holds the result. For example, with a 3. 3 volts reference and 1. 234 volts in, the first trial is 1.
65 volts, which is too high, so the MSB is 0. Next trial is 0. 825 volts, input is above, keep it. Then 1. 2375 volts, too high, drop it. And so on.
Ten steps give a 10-bit code of 382.
That's why it's so popular in microcontrollers: one comparator and a capacitor array, no static power, N clock cycles per conversion, so you get 100 kS/s to a few MS/s at 10 to 16 bits.

The things to watch are that the input has to be held steady during the search, that the source impedance has to be low enough for the sampling cap to charge, and that the reference needs to supply charge each step, so it needs good decoupling."
